Posterior Maps, Remote-Sensing Change, and Decision Products

bayesAgriFlow

Source: vignettes/v39-posterior-maps-and-change.Rmd
v39-posterior-maps-and-change.Rmd

Purpose

A remote-sensing workflow often ends with a map, but a Bayesian map should communicate a posterior quantity rather than an aesthetically smooth surface. Version 1.3.0 therefore separates posterior prediction, uncertainty summarization, map-ready formatting, threshold probability, and change analysis. The spatial and temporal interpretation follows the process-oriented principles introduced in the 1.2.0 spatiotemporal module (Cressie and Wikle 2011).

1. A map needs an estimand

Before mapping, name the quantity: expected biomass, predictive observation, posterior SD, credible interval width, probability of stress, or change between dates. Different quantities answer different questions and should not share an ambiguous legend such as “prediction.”

Interpretation checklist

  • Name the posterior quantity in the map title and legend.
  • State the response units.
  • Identify the spatial support of each map cell or point.

2. Posterior mean prediction

bayes_rs_predict(type = "mean") targets the posterior expected response conditional on model inputs. It does not include new observation noise in the same way as posterior predictive draws.

if (FALSE) {
  pred <- bayes_rs_predict(fit, newdata = prediction_grid, type = "mean")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Use posterior mean predictions for expected latent response.
  • Use predictive observations when future measurement variability matters.

3. Posterior predictive observations

type = "predictive" propagates observation-level variability. The interval is therefore usually wider. This distinction matters when maps are used to predict what a new field measurement might record.

if (FALSE) {
  pred_y <- bayes_rs_predict(fit, prediction_grid, type = "predictive")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Do not compare mean and predictive intervals as if they estimate the same quantity.
  • State which type is mapped.

4. Map-ready data

bayes_rs_map() converts a prediction result into a simple x, y, value table. This dependency-light default keeps plotting choice open. If terra is available and the prediction points form a suitable grid, as_raster = TRUE can create a SpatRaster.

if (FALSE) {
  m <- bayes_rs_map(pred, quantity = "mean")
  mr <- bayes_rs_map(pred, quantity = "mean", as_raster = TRUE, crs = "EPSG:31985")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Check that prediction points form the intended grid before rasterizing.
  • Do not create artificial resolution by oversampling a smooth model.
  • Carry the CRS explicitly.

5. Uncertainty map

A posterior mean map without uncertainty can imply false precision. bayes_rs_uncertainty() calculates posterior SD and interval width at every prediction location; bayes_rs_map() can then format either quantity.

if (FALSE) {
  unc <- bayes_rs_uncertainty(pred)
  m_sd <- bayes_rs_map(pred, quantity = "posterior_sd")
  m_w  <- bayes_rs_map(pred, quantity = "interval_width")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Present uncertainty in response units when possible.
  • Inspect whether uncertainty increases near domain edges.
  • Flag extrapolation regions separately.

6. Threshold probability

Many agronomic decisions are naturally probabilistic. A stress map can show P(Y < c | data) rather than coloring expected values below an arbitrary cutoff. This retains uncertainty around the threshold.

if (FALSE) {
  stress <- bayes_rs_uncertainty(pred, threshold = 0.35, direction = "below")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Predefine a scientifically meaningful threshold.
  • Report the probability itself rather than only a binary classification.
  • Connect the threshold to an explicit intervention or interpretation.

7. Spatial extrapolation

Gaussian-process prediction can look smooth outside dense sampling. Smoothness is not evidence. Prediction grids should identify distances from observed data or other extrapolation diagnostics when the map extends beyond the sampled field.

Interpretation checklist

  • Differentiate interpolation from extrapolation.
  • Do not crop the uncertainty legend to hide high-uncertainty areas.
  • Consider restricting operational maps to a supported domain.

8. Temporal extrapolation

Remote-sensing forecasts beyond observed acquisition times are different from interpolation between dates. The 1.3.0 model uses the same explicit temporal structures as the spatiotemporal layer; future predictions should be labeled as forecasts.

sat <- bayes_teaching_data("satellite")
range(sat$day)

Interpretation checklist

  • Report the forecast horizon.
  • State the temporal model.
  • Avoid long-horizon extrapolation from a short acquisition series.

9. Change is a posterior contrast

bayes_rs_change() predicts matched locations at two acquisition times and subtracts the posterior draws. This preserves covariance between model parameters and yields a posterior distribution of change rather than subtracting two unrelated summary maps.

if (FALSE) {
  ch <- bayes_rs_change(
    fit, newdata = grid_two_dates,
    baseline_time = 14, comparison_time = 28,
    threshold = 0.5
  )
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Compare the same spatial locations.
  • Interpret the sign consistently.
  • Report credible intervals and probability of meaningful change.

10. Meaningful change threshold

A zero threshold asks whether change is positive. An agronomically meaningful threshold asks whether change is large enough to matter. bayes_rs_change() reports the posterior probability that the difference exceeds the requested threshold.

if (FALSE) {
  ch05 <- bayes_rs_change(fit, grid_two_dates, 14, 28, threshold = 0.5)
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Define meaningful change in response units.
  • Perform sensitivity analysis over plausible thresholds if needed.
  • Do not equate high probability of tiny change with practical importance.

11. Change versus sensor drift

Apparent temporal change can arise from platform calibration, illumination, atmospheric conditions, georegistration, or preprocessing differences. A Bayesian change model propagates model uncertainty but cannot correct undocumented acquisition bias automatically.

Interpretation checklist

  • Check inter-date sensor calibration.
  • Use stable references when available.
  • Do not interpret acquisition artifacts as biology.

12. Mapping treatment contrasts

When the fitted model contains experimental treatments, posterior predictions can be generated under treatment-specific scenarios and contrasted. The map should distinguish treatment-effect surfaces from observed treatment assignments.

if (FALSE) {
  # Build two matched prediction grids differing only in treatment.
  pA <- bayes_rs_predict(fit, grid_A)
  pB <- bayes_rs_predict(fit, grid_B)
  treatment_difference_draws <- pA$draws - pB$draws
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Use matched covariates for causal-style contrasts in randomized experiments.
  • Do not infer treatment effects from spatial association alone.
  • Respect the original randomization.

13. Decision maps

A posterior probability map can feed a scouting or intervention rule, but the optimal action also depends on costs and consequences. The existing decision layer can translate posterior outcomes into expected utility and regret.

Interpretation checklist

  • Separate statistical risk from economic utility.
  • State false-positive and false-negative consequences.
  • Avoid a universal probability cutoff.

14. Map validation

Maps should be validated using held-out support that resembles intended deployment. Pixel-wise random cross-validation can be optimistic under spatial autocorrelation. Plot, block, date, or spatial-region holdout may be more honest.

Interpretation checklist

  • Choose holdout units before fitting when possible.
  • Report spatial and temporal separation of validation data.
  • Use prediction intervals as well as point error metrics.

15. Export without losing provenance

The default map object is a small data frame with a quantity attribute. If exported to GIS, accompany it with model version, response units, posterior quantity, interval level, prediction date, CRS, and source table hash.

if (FALSE) {
  map_df <- bayes_rs_map(pred, quantity = "mean")
  attr(map_df, "quantity")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Version the map and source model together.
  • Keep human-readable metadata beside raster files.
  • Archive hashes for frozen release products.

16. Integrated monitoring workflow

Repeated remote-sensing acquisitions can be treated as a monitoring system. The workflow should preserve the distinction between current-state estimation, future prediction, change detection, and decision support.

sat <- bayes_teaching_data("satellite")
des <- bayes_rs_model(sat, "biomass", c("ndvi","evi"), x_coord="x", y_coord="y", time="day", subject="location_id", temporal="ar1")
if (FALSE) {
  fit <- bayes_fit(des, engine="brms", compute=bayes_compute(backend="cmdstanr"))
  pred <- bayes_rs_predict(fit, monitoring_grid)
  unc <- bayes_rs_uncertainty(pred, threshold=stress_limit, direction="below")
  ch <- bayes_rs_change(fit, two_date_grid, 14, 28, threshold=.5)
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Estimate current state.
  • Quantify uncertainty.
  • Assess meaningful change.
  • Forecast only when required.
  • Translate posterior quantities into decisions explicitly.

17. What not to infer from a beautiful map

A smooth, colorful posterior surface does not establish causal effect, external validity, sensor accuracy, or biological mechanism. Those claims require design, calibration, validation, and substantive evidence beyond visualization.

Interpretation checklist

  • Do not use cartographic polish as evidence.
  • Report data density and uncertainty.
  • Keep causal language for causally identified analyses.

Final checklist

  • The map title names a posterior quantity.
  • Units, CRS, date, and spatial support are documented.
  • Posterior uncertainty is available beside the mean.
  • Thresholds have scientific meaning.
  • Change maps compare matched locations.
  • Sensor drift and preprocessing differences were considered.
  • Validation reflects deployment support.
  • Decision thresholds are tied to consequences.
  • The frozen source model can be reconstructed.

Map-release audit worksheet

Before distributing a posterior map, verify all of the following.

  1. The response and its units are named.
  2. The mapped posterior quantity is named.
  3. The credible interval level is documented.
  4. The coordinate reference system is documented.
  5. The prediction date or time is documented.
  6. Interpolation and extrapolation regions are distinguishable.
  7. The spatial support of each value is documented.
  8. An uncertainty product accompanies the mean product.
  9. Thresholds are scientifically justified.
  10. Change maps compare matched spatial locations.
  11. Sensor calibration across dates was considered.
  12. Validation reflects spatial and temporal dependence.
  13. The map is linked to a frozen model and source-data version.
  14. Decision rules are reported separately from posterior probabilities.
  15. Causal language is used only when the design supports it.

A posterior map is a statistical product with assumptions and provenance, not an independent observation of the field.

Cressie, Noel, and Christopher K. Wikle. 2011. Statistics for Spatio-Temporal Data. Wiley.
